Edge footprint (as published): Closed-form fusion is negligible in cost; per-view encoders dominate; plausible on Pi-class CPU with small encoders.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: evidential fusion and conflict signal for the orchestrator.

Task: Trustworthy multimodal classification with per-sample dynamic fusion.
Method: Sparse feature gating plus true-class-probability modality confidence; confidence-weighted fusion.
Setup and data: Multimodal medical classification datasets (multi-omics).
Key result: Reported superior performance and trustworthiness versus prior methods (no figures in the abstract).
Limitation: Medical/tabular domain; confidence estimator itself may be miscalibrated.
Edge footprint (as published): Lightweight gating and weighting; small models plausible on Pi-class CPU.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / component: learnt confidence-weighted fusion versus evidential fusion.

Task: Safe planning among dynamic agents with probabilistic guarantees.
Method: MPC with conformal-prediction regions around learnt trajectory predictions.
Setup and data: CARLA simulator, pedestrian-filled intersection.
Key result: Valid probabilistic safety guarantees demonstrated; no numeric results in the abstract.
Limitation: Simulation only; requires exchangeable calibration data.
Edge footprint (as published): Conformal calibration is cheap; MPC and predictor cost depend on horizon and model; small instances plausible on a Pi-class CPU.
Role in the framework: Confidence-signal source: distribution-free calibration of module outputs.

Task: Confidence calibration of VLA robot policies.
Method: Calibration analysis; prompt ensembles and action-wise Platt scaling.
Setup and data: VLA models on manipulation tasks (benchmarks not named in the abstract).
Key result: Miscalibration observed and reduced by proposed remedies (no figures in the abstract).
Limitation: Post-hoc; needs labelled calibration episodes; evaluated on existing VLAs.
Edge footprint (as published): Platt scaling is negligible; prompt ensembles multiply VLA inference cost, and VLAs themselves typically need a GPU rather than a Raspberry Pi.
Role in the framework: Confidence-signal source: calibration of imitation-module confidence.

Task: Epistemic uncertainty for flow-matching VLAs; failure detection and active fine-tuning.
Method: Velocity-field disagreement across a small ensemble; SAVE uncertainty-guided data acquisition.
Setup and data: LIBERO simulated manipulation benchmark.
Key result: Better-calibrated uncertainty; strong failure detection; at least 22% fewer samples than baselines.
Limitation: Simulation only (per abstract); ensemble overhead.
Edge footprint (as published): Requires running a VLA plus several action heads; GPU-class compute rather than a Raspberry Pi, though a small ensemble of heads over a shared backbone limits overhead.
Role in the framework: Confidence-signal source: epistemic uncertainty for the imitation module; reference for uncertainty-guided data requests.

Task: Deployment-time policy steering under semantic and action uncertainty.
Method: VLM verifier over policy samples, conformal calibration, three-way act/ask/intervene choice, residual learning.
Setup and data: Simulation and real hardware (robot not stated in abstract).
Key result: Disentangles confident, ambiguous and incapable cases; fewer interventions than baselines (no figures in the abstract).
Limitation: Requires human feedback and a large VLM verifier.
Edge footprint (as published): VLM verifier and diffusion policy imply GPU or remote compute; the conformal decision layer itself is cheap.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / baseline to beat: calibrated arbitration between act, ask and learn.

Task: Efficient sampling from replay memory in deep RL.
Method: Prioritised sampling of transitions by expected learning progress, applied to DQN.
Setup and data: Atari 2600 benchmark, 49 games.
Key result: Outperforms uniform-replay DQN on 41 of 49 games; state of the art at the time.
Limitation: Sampling bias; priority bookkeeping; discrete-action games only.
Edge footprint (as published): Replay prioritisation adds modest memory and a sum-tree lookup; feasible on a Pi-class CPU for small buffers, while the DQN training used GPU-class compute.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: prioritised replay for online updates of modules and orchestrator.

Task: Continual RL with transfer and without forgetting.
Method: Progressive columns with frozen predecessors and lateral connections.
Setup and data: Atari and 3D maze RL tasks.
Key result: Outperforms pretrain-and-finetune baselines; transfer at sensory and control layers.
Limitation: Parameters grow linearly with tasks.
Edge footprint (as published): Each task adds a full column; memory growth makes long task sequences unsuitable for a Raspberry Pi; training used GPU-class compute.
Role in the framework: Competing approach: architectural isolation versus adapter-based updates.

Task: Sequential learning without catastrophic forgetting.
Method: Elastic weight consolidation: Fisher-weighted quadratic penalty towards previous parameters.
Setup and data: Permuted/sequential MNIST classification; sequential Atari 2600 games.
Key result: Retains performance on earlier tasks (no figures in the abstract).
Limitation: Diagonal Fisher approximation; needs task boundaries; weakens over long sequences.
Edge footprint (as published): Stores one extra copy of parameters and a diagonal Fisher; memory doubles but compute is small; feasible on a Pi for small networks or adapters.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / baseline: regulariser for online adapter updates.

Task: Continual learning from a single pass over task sequences.
Method: Metrics for backward/forward transfer; GEM gradient projection using episodic memory.
Setup and data: MNIST variants and CIFAR-100.
Key result: Strong performance versus state of the art (no figures in the abstract).
Limitation: QP cost scales with tasks; needs task labels.
Edge footprint (as published): Requires per-step gradients on memory samples and a small QP; feasible for small models on a Pi but costlier than plain SGD.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference (transfer metrics) and competing approach for safe updates.

Task: Class-incremental learning of classifiers and representations.
Method: Exemplar memory with herding, nearest-mean-of-exemplars classification, distillation.
Setup and data: CIFAR-100 and ImageNet ILSVRC 2012.
Key result: Learns many classes incrementally where other strategies fail (no figures in the abstract).
Limitation: Needs exemplar storage; image classification only.
Edge footprint (as published): Exemplar buffer and small CNN updates feasible on Pi-class storage; training speed on CPU would be slow.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: incremental extension of the perception module.

Task: Parameter-efficient transfer of pretrained Transformers.
Method: Bottleneck adapter layers in each block; frozen backbone.
Setup and data: BERT on 26 text-classification tasks including GLUE.
Key result: Within 0.4% of full fine-tuning on GLUE with 3.6% added parameters per task.
Limitation: Adds inference latency; NLP only.
Edge footprint (as published): Adapter training on a frozen backbone reduces memory, but BERT-scale training used GPUs; small adapters are storable per task on a Pi.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / baseline: adapter-based per-task updates.

Task: Continual RL without task boundaries.
Method: Replay of all past experience with mixed on/off-policy learning and behavioural cloning (CLEAR).
Setup and data: Atari and DMLab task sequences.
Key result: Substantially reduced forgetting; matches task-aware methods; random-discard buffer nearly as good as unbounded.
Limitation: Simulated games; replay storage still substantial.
Edge footprint (as published): Replay buffers fit on a Pi's storage if bounded; the RL training in the paper used large-scale distributed compute.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / baseline to beat: replay with random eviction for online updates.

Task: Memory-efficient on-device transfer learning.
Method: Frozen weights, bias-only updates, lite residual modules.
Setup and data: Image-classification transfer learning benchmarks.
Key result: Up to 6.5x memory saving; up to 34.1% over last-layer tuning; 7.3–12.9x saving vs full Inception-V3 fine-tuning.
Limitation: Image classification only.
Edge footprint (as published): Designed for edge devices; memory-light enough in principle for a Raspberry Pi-class device, though the paper's hardware targets are not stated in the abstract.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: activation-memory-aware on-device fine-tuning of perception modules.

Task: Deep-learning inference on microcontrollers.
Method: TinyNAS architecture search co-designed with TinyEngine inference library.
Setup and data: ImageNet and visual/audio wake-word tasks on commercial MCUs.
Key result: >70% ImageNet top-1 on MCU; 4.8x memory and 1.7–3.3x speed gains; 3.5x less SRAM, 5.7x less Flash.
Limitation: Inference only; no on-device training.
Edge footprint (as published): Runs on microcontrollers, far below a Raspberry Pi 5; architecture search itself is offline and compute-heavy.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: efficient perception backbones for the Pi-based robot.

Task: Parameter-efficient adaptation for text generation.
Method: Trainable continuous prefix vectors with frozen LM.
Setup and data: GPT-2 table-to-text; BART summarisation.
Key result: 0.1% parameters; comparable in full data, better in low data and on unseen topics.
Limitation: Consumes context length; text generation only.
Edge footprint (as published): Tiny trainable state; training still needs backpropagation through the frozen LM, so GPU-class for large models, possibly CPU for very small LMs.
Role in the framework: Competing approach to LoRA for orchestrator adaptation.

Task: Parameter-efficient adaptation of large language models.
Method: Frozen weights plus trainable low-rank update matrices per layer; mergeable at inference.
Setup and data: RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, GPT-3 on NLP benchmarks.
Key result: 10,000x fewer trainable parameters and 3x less GPU memory than full GPT-3 fine-tuning; on-par or better quality; no added latency.
Limitation: Rank/layer choice; activation and base-model memory remain.
Edge footprint (as published): Adapters are megabytes and add no inference latency; training small (≤1B) models with LoRA may be feasible on a Pi 5 CPU but slowly, larger models need a GPU.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: core online-adaptation mechanism for the orchestrator.

Task: On-device training under 256 KB memory.
Method: Quantisation-Aware Scaling; Sparse Update; Tiny Training Engine with compile-time autodiff.
Setup and data: Microcontroller-class devices; tinyML tasks including VWW.
Key result: Training within 256 KB SRAM and 1 MB Flash; <1/1000 memory of PyTorch/TensorFlow; matches accuracy on VWW.
Limitation: Small CNNs; sparse-update schedule chosen offline.
Edge footprint (as published): Runs on microcontrollers, far below a Raspberry Pi 5 budget.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: sparse, memory-bounded on-device updates for perception modules.

Task: Comparing few-shot ICL with parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
Method: (IA)³ activation-scaling PEFT; T-Few recipe on T0.
Setup and data: NLP tasks; RAFT benchmark.
Key result: Super-human on RAFT; +6% absolute over prior state of the art; lower compute than ICL.
Limitation: NLP only; T0-scale models.
Edge footprint (as published): PEFT reduces inference cost relative to long ICL prompts; T0-scale training needs GPUs, not a Pi.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference: evidence for fine-tuning over prompting in the orchestrator.

Task: Memory-efficient fine-tuning of quantised LLMs.
Method: 4-bit frozen base model with LoRA adapters; backprop through quantised weights.
Setup and data: LLaMA and other model families up to 65B; instruction datasets; Vicuna benchmark.
Key result: 65B model fine-tuned on one 48 GB GPU; Guanaco reaches 99.3% of ChatGPT on Vicuna after 24 h on one GPU.
Limitation: CUDA-dependent training; chatbot-style evaluation.
Edge footprint (as published): Needs a GPU for training at the reported scale; 4-bit inference of small models fits a Raspberry Pi 5, but on-Pi QLoRA training is not demonstrated.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: quantised base plus LoRA for the local orchestrator.

Task: Human-in-the-loop deployment and learning for manipulation.
Method: Shared autonomy with human intervention; trust-weighted behavioural cloning on deployment data.
Setup and data: Contact-rich manipulation in simulation and on a real robot.
Key result: +8% (sim) and +27% (real) success over SOTA; 2x faster convergence; 85% memory reduction.
Limitation: Requires a human monitor.
Edge footprint (as published): Behavioural-cloning policies of moderate size; training likely on a GPU; the 85% memory reduction concerns the data buffer.
Role in the framework: Baseline to beat / confidence-signal source: intervention-weighted imitation during deployment.

Task: Benchmark for lifelong robot learning.
Method: Procedural task generation; four task suites with human demonstrations; benchmarking of architectures and algorithms.
Setup and data: Simulated tabletop manipulation; 130 tasks in four suites.
Key result: Sequential fine-tuning beats lifelong methods in forward transfer; no encoder dominates; supervised pretraining can hurt.
Limitation: Simulation only; single-arm tabletop; demonstration-dependent.
Edge footprint (as published): Simulation benchmark requiring a desktop GPU for policy training; not intended to run on a Pi.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference: standard continual imitation-learning benchmark.

Task: Efficient sparse on-device fine-tuning across edge hardware.
Method: Compilation-first training graphs; sparse back-propagation; operator reordering and backend switching.
Setup and data: Raspberry Pi, Jetson AGX Orin, mobile CPU/GPU/DSP; vision and LLM models.
Key result: Up to 15x speed-up vs TensorFlow on Raspberry Pi; 5.6x memory saving on Jetson Orin; LLaMA-2-7B fine-tuning at 550 tokens/s (7.9x vs PyTorch).
Limitation: Per-model sparse schemes; LLM results need Jetson-class GPU.
Edge footprint (as published): Explicitly demonstrated on Raspberry Pi for smaller models; 7B LLM fine-tuning needs a Jetson AGX Orin, not a Pi.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: on-device training engine for modules and orchestrator.

Task: Memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning.
Method: In-place zeroth-order SGD using forward passes only (MeZO).
Setup and data: Masked and autoregressive LMs up to 66B; classification, multiple choice and generation.
Key result: 30B model on one A100 80GB; up to 12x memory reduction; up to 2x fewer GPU-hours; comparable to backprop.
Limitation: More optimisation steps needed; evaluated on GPUs.
Edge footprint (as published): Inference-level memory makes on-Pi fine-tuning of small LMs plausible, but step count implies long wall-clock time on a CPU.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / competing approach to LoRA backprop for on-robot orchestrator updates.

Task: Continual adaptation of pretrained policies to new manipulation tasks.
Method: Task-specific PEFT modules (adapters, P-Tuning, LoRA) on a frozen pretrained policy.
Setup and data: Large-scale language-conditioned manipulation tasks (simulated; suite not named in the abstract).
Key result: LoRA best post-adaptation performance with 1% of full fine-tuning parameters; no catastrophic forgetting.
Limitation: No real-robot evaluation reported in abstract; needs task identity for adapter selection.
Edge footprint (as published): Per-task adapters are small; training the base policy and adapters used GPUs; per-task inference could fit an edge device if the base model is small.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / baseline: LoRA per-task adapters for imitation module.

Task: Continual imitation learning for manipulation.
Method: Continual unsupervised skill discovery with an open-vocabulary vision model; growing skill library; meta-controller composing skills.
Setup and data: Vision-based manipulation task sequences with few demonstrations per task (benchmark not named in the abstract).
Key result: Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by over 11% in success rate.
Limitation: Needs demonstrations; heavy vision model; assumes recurring skill structure.
Edge footprint (as published): Open-vocabulary vision model and policy training imply GPU compute; skill-selection meta-controller itself is light.
Role in the framework: Competing approach: meta-controller over skills, analogous to orchestration over modalities.

Task: LLM fine-tuning on resource-constrained mobile devices.
Method: Server-assisted side-tuning: frozen on-device backbone, server-side adapter back-propagation, quantised activation transfer.
Setup and data: Mobile devices including CPU-only; LLM fine-tuning tasks (details not given in the abstract).
Key result: Enables fine-tuning on CPU-only devices; reduced convergence time and memory (no figures in the abstract).
Limitation: Requires a high-performance server; network dependence.
Edge footprint (as published): Device runs only forward passes of a frozen LLM; feasible on a Pi-class CPU for small LLMs, but training relies on a remote GPU server.
Role in the framework: Competing approach: server-assisted versus fully local adaptation.

Task: Exemplar-free continual learning for VLAs.
Method: Modular adapters in feed-forward layers with similarity-guided expansion; autoencoder-based task-agnostic routing.
Setup and data: LIBERO simulated manipulation benchmark.
Key result: Strong new-task performance with mitigated forgetting; surpasses exemplar-based baselines (no figures in the abstract).
Limitation: Simulation (as summarised); adapter growth with task diversity.
Edge footprint (as published): Base VLA inference and training require a GPU; adapters and autoencoder routers are small.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / baseline to beat: adapter routing as familiarity signal and expansion rule.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Modular supervised learning with specialised expert networks.
Method: Gating network assigning input-dependent responsibilities to competing experts.
Setup and data: Supervised task (vowel discrimination).
Key result: Experts specialise on input subsets (no figures in the abstract).
Limitation: Small scale; gate instability; no compute-cost treatment.
Edge footprint (as published): Tiny networks by modern standards; trivially runs on a Pi.
Role in the framework: Conceptual foundation: orchestrator as gating network over modalities.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Reduce inference/training cost of deep networks via input-dependent activation of unit blocks.
Method: RL (policy gradient) over block-dropout masks with a sparsity/speed-motivated loss and a diversity regulariser.
Setup and data: Fully connected classifiers on MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN; CPU and GPU timing.
Key result: Abstract reports improved computation speed without loss of approximation quality; speed-ups larger on CPU than GPU (per the full text; exact figures not quoted here).
Limitation: Small-scale classifiers only; high-variance policy-gradient training; speed-ups depend on sparse-kernel hardware support.
Edge footprint (as published): Tiny MLPs; policy adds negligible overhead; CPU-friendly and plausible on a Pi-class device, though gains depend on block-sparse kernels.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / conceptual precursor: learned per-input computation gating under a cost penalty, analogous to budgeted modality selection.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Let RNNs learn a variable number of computation steps per input.
Method: Sigmoidal halting unit with cumulative-probability threshold, mean-field state averaging, and a ponder-cost penalty weighted by τ.
Setup and data: Synthetic parity, logic, addition, sorting tasks; character-level Wikipedia (Hutter Prize) language modelling.
Key result: Dramatic gains on synthetic tasks; little gain on Wikipedia modelling but interpretable allocation of steps at word/punctuation boundaries.
Limitation: Requires per-task tuning of τ; sequence tasks only; no hardware latency evaluation.
Edge footprint (as published): Small LSTMs; halting unit is negligible overhead; conceptually portable to CPU-class edge devices.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / conceptual component: differentiable adaptive-compute penalty reusable as a budget term in the orchestrator objective.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Increase model capacity without proportional compute via conditional computation.
Method: Sparsely-gated MoE layer with trainable noisy top-k gating and load-balancing auxiliary losses, placed between stacked LSTMs.
Setup and data: Large-scale language modelling and machine translation benchmarks on GPU clusters; MoE up to 137B parameters.
Key result: >1000x capacity increase with minor efficiency loss; significantly better than state of the art at lower computational cost (abstract).
Limitation: Requires distributed GPU clusters; routing instability and load imbalance; not evaluated on embodied tasks.
Edge footprint (as published): Datacentre-scale (up to 137B parameters on GPU clusters); the gating mechanism itself is cheap, but the models are far beyond Pi-class hardware.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse (conceptually): sparse top-k gating with load balancing as the template for a learned modality router.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Multi-task learning without task interference via dynamic composition of modules.
Method: Router + function blocks; recursive per-input routing to fixed depth; router trained with collaborative multi-agent RL, blocks by SGD.
Setup and data: Multi-task MNIST, mini-ImageNet, CIFAR-100; baselines cross-stitch and shared-layer networks.
Key result: Significant accuracy gains, sharper convergence; ~constant per-task training cost; cross-stitch performance with 85% less training time on CIFAR-100 (20 tasks).
Limitation: Small image benchmarks; fixed recursion depth; RL router training can be unstable; no robotics evaluation.
Edge footprint (as published): Small CNN/MLP blocks and lightweight router; inference cost comparable to a single path, feasible on CPU-class edge hardware.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / design reference: RL-trained router selecting among reusable modules, close to learning which modality to invoke.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Scale vision transformers with sparse conditional computation.
Method: V-MoE: sparse MoE layers in ViT; Batch Prioritised Routing for adaptive per-image compute.
Setup and data: Large-scale image recognition pre-training; ImageNet evaluation.
Key result: Matches SOTA with as little as half the inference compute; 15B-parameter model reaches 90.35% on ImageNet.
Limitation: Requires massive pre-training and accelerator infrastructure; routing benefits tied to large models.
Edge footprint (as published): Billions of parameters trained on accelerators; far beyond a Raspberry Pi 5, though the priority-routing idea is transferable.
Role in the framework: Evaluation/design reference: test-time compute–accuracy trade-off via routing, a pattern for budget-adjustable perception.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Budget-aware interactive imitation learning with limited human interventions.
Method: Learned switching policy gated on state novelty and estimated risk (low confidence of task completion) under an intervention budget.
Setup and data: Simulated task and physical cable routing; user study (N=10) supervising a three-robot fleet.
Key result: 100% execution-time success in sim and physical tasks; +58% human and +80% robot performance vs next-best algorithm in user study.
Limitation: Requires a human supervisor; thresholds must be tuned to the budget; limited task diversity.
Edge footprint (as published): Novelty/risk estimators are small networks; gating is cheap and plausibly runs on a Pi-class robot alongside the policy.
Role in the framework: Confidence-signal source / component to reuse: novelty and risk gating under an explicit budget, directly analogous to modality escalation.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Scale sparse MoE language models with simpler, more stable routing.
Method: Top-1 ('switch') routing, reduced communication, stability techniques, bfloat16 training.
Setup and data: T5-based pre-training on C4; multilingual mT5 comparison across 101 languages.
Key result: Up to 7x pre-training speed-up vs T5-Base/Large; 4x speed-up over T5-XXL at trillion-parameter scale.
Limitation: Requires large accelerator clusters; language-only; instability and fine-tuning issues remain at scale.
Edge footprint (as published): Datacentre-scale training; not deployable on Pi-class hardware, though top-1 routing is computationally trivial.
Role in the framework: Design reference: evidence that single-expert (top-1) routing is effective, supporting a discrete modality choice.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Differentiable, stable mixture-of-experts routing for vision transformers.
Method: Soft MoE: each expert slot receives a learned weighted mixture of all tokens.
Setup and data: Large-scale visual recognition; comparisons with dense ViT, Tokens Choice and Experts Choice MoE.
Key result: Soft MoE Huge/14 (128 experts, 16 MoE layers): >40x parameters of ViT-H/14 with only 2% more inference time and better quality.
Limitation: Token mixing complicates causal/autoregressive use; evaluated only at large scale on vision.
Edge footprint (as published): Large vision models on accelerators; not Pi-deployable as reported, though routing overhead itself is modest.
Role in the framework: Competing approach: soft differentiable routing as an alternative to hard modality selection.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Multitask and continual robot imitation learning with low active compute and no forgetting.
Method: Transformer diffusion policy with task-specific routers over MoE expert layers; freeze-and-add experts for continual learning; expert recombination for transfer.
Setup and data: MimicGen (8 tasks), DexArt, Adroit simulation; continual learning and coffee-preparation transfer; real-robot pulling, pick-and-place, hanging.
Key result: 0.76 avg success on MimicGen with 53.3M active params (vs 52.6M single-task); 0.94 retained success in continual learning at 9.2M active params; 0.80 transfer success with 0.1M trainable params vs 0.70 from scratch.
Limitation: Routing conditioned on known task identity; limited real-robot evaluation; diffusion sampling latency remains.
Edge footprint (as published): Tens of millions of active parameters with iterative diffusion denoising; GPU training; inference on a Pi 5 would be slow without distillation/fewer steps.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: sparse, freeze-and-add expert structure for the imitation modality, enabling skill growth without forgetting.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Reduce the monetary cost of querying LLM APIs while keeping or improving accuracy.
Method: LLM cascade with a learned answer-reliability scorer and budget-optimised model ordering and stopping thresholds.
Setup and data: Commercial LLM APIs (e.g. GPT-4, ChatGPT, J1-Jumbo) on natural-language query datasets.
Key result: Matches best single LLM (GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction, or +4% accuracy over GPT-4 at equal cost.
Limitation: Per-task scorer training; cloud-API setting; single-turn text tasks, not sequential control.
Edge footprint (as published): Relies on cloud LLM APIs; the scorer itself is small and edge-feasible, but the cascaded models are not local.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / design template: confidence-gated cascade escalation, directly mappable to cheap-to-expensive modality escalation on-device.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Route queries between a small edge-deployable LLM and a large cloud LLM to save cost at controlled quality.
Method: Learned router predicting whether the small model's quality is close to the large model's; test-time tunable threshold.
Setup and data: Instruction-following queries; small/large pairs such as Llama-2 variants vs GPT-3.5-turbo.
Key result: Up to 40% fewer large-model calls with no quality drop; router ~0.036 s vs 0.46–14.61 s LLM latency (full text).
Limitation: Relies on automatic quality metrics; binary routing only; single-turn text tasks.
Edge footprint (as published): Router is a small encoder with millisecond-scale latency; the small LLM side is edge-oriented, but the fallback is cloud-based.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / component to reuse: calibrated difficulty router with a tunable quality–cost threshold for local-first escalation.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Cost-efficient routing among LLMs of different sizes based on self-assessed answer correctness.
Method: Few-shot self-verification by the small model plus a POMDP-based router that treats verifier confidence as a noisy observation.
Setup and data: Five language models and five context-grounded reasoning/QA datasets.
Key result: Over 50% reduction in computational cost for comparable performance; consistently beats strong baselines.
Limitation: Self-verification needs context-grounded tasks; extra verification calls; text-only evaluation.
Edge footprint (as published): Router is lightweight; verification uses the small LM itself, so feasible with a small local LM, though larger fallbacks are cloud-hosted in the paper.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / component to reuse: POMDP router over noisy self-confidence, a model for fusing imperfect confidence signals.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Reduce compute and memory of MLLM-based robot VLA policies under resource constraints.
Method: Multi-exit MLLM with early-termination criteria conditioned on average compute, peak compute (latency) and GPU memory budgets.
Setup and data: CALVIN simulated long-horizon language-conditioned manipulation benchmark.
Key result: 5.2–6.5x reduction in LLM computational cost and 2–6x reduction in LLM GPU memory without performance loss.
Limitation: Simulation only; exit thresholds set offline; still requires a GPU-class device.
Edge footprint (as published): Billion-parameter MLLM; savings are relative and still GPU-bound; not directly Pi 5-deployable, though the budget-conditioned exit logic is.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / evaluation reference: budget-conditioned dynamic inference for robot policies; baseline for compute-aware switching.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Efficient, scalable diffusion policies for multitask imitation learning.
Method: Mixture-of-Denoising-Experts with noise-conditioned routing and self-attention; expert caching for inference.
Setup and data: CALVIN and LIBERO benchmarks (134 tasks across four benchmarks); optional pre-training on diverse robot data.
Key result: −40% active parameters, −90% inference cost; CALVIN ABC 4.01, LIBERO-90 0.95; +57% average over diffusion baselines with 90% fewer FLOPs.
Limitation: Simulation benchmarks; routing is by noise level rather than task or state.
Edge footprint (as published): Reduced FLOPs and caching make inference far cheaper than dense diffusion transformers; still likely needs a GPU or careful optimisation for Pi 5.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / baseline: efficient multitask imitation policy with low inference cost.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Multitask legged locomotion over diverse terrains and gaits with a single policy.
Method: Multitask PPO-style RL with MoE layers in actor/critic to mitigate gradient conflicts; expert specialisation used for skill composition and migration.
Setup and data: IsaacGym (4,096 parallel robots, 6 experts); Unitree Go2 with Jetson Orin; 9 tasks (5 quadrupedal, 4 bipedal).
Key result: 87.9% mixed-terrain success in simulation; successful real deployment across all 9 tasks; reduced gradient conflict.
Limitation: Locomotion only; sim-to-real with privileged training; limited quantitative real-world reporting.
Edge footprint (as published): Runs onboard at 50 Hz on a Jetson Orin (embedded GPU); small MLP experts suggest CPU feasibility, but not tested on Pi-class hardware.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference / design reference: real-robot evidence that expert specialisation reduces multitask interference.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Learn routers that choose between a strong and a weak LLM per query to trade cost against quality.
Method: Routers trained on human preference data (plus data augmentation) predicting the strong model's win probability; threshold sets the operating point.
Setup and data: Standard LLM benchmarks; strong/weak model pairs; transfer to unseen model pairs.
Key result: Cost reductions of over 2x in some cases without quality loss; routers transfer when model pairs change.
Limitation: Binary routing only; preference-data domain mismatch; text-only.
Edge footprint (as published): Routers are lightweight and cheap enough for edge CPU; the routed LLMs are large/cloud-hosted in the paper.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / component to reuse: learning a router from comparative outcome data that transfers across swapped modules.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Scalable, transferable multi-task manipulation with diffusion policies at low inference cost.
Method: Diffusion MoE policy with an orthogonal skill basis, sticky routing, variational objective and adaptive expert activation.
Setup and data: Simulation benchmarks (MetaWorld mentioned in summary) and a real dual-arm platform; multi-task and transfer experiments.
Key result: Higher success rates and markedly lower inference cost than large diffusion baselines (no figures in abstract).
Limitation: No quantitative figures in the abstract; requires diverse demonstrations to learn a reusable skill basis.
Edge footprint (as published): Designed to reduce active parameters and latency; still a diffusion policy, likely GPU-trained; Pi-class inference untested.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / design reference: sticky, phase-consistent sparse expert activation for imitation skills, informing switching hysteresis.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Decide when an embodied LLM agent should reason versus act, under resource constraints.
Method: RARRL: hierarchical framework with an RL-trained high-level policy deciding whether/how much to invoke LLM reasoning, trading success against latency/tokens.
Setup and data: ALFRED benchmark in AI2-THOR; navigation, inspection, multi-step delivery tasks.
Key result: >60% lower LLM inference time and 50–75% fewer tokens; success e.g. 82.7±1.7% vs 84.0% (navigation), 76.4±1.9% vs 78.5% (inspection), 69.5±2.1% vs 71.2% (delivery).
Limitation: Simulation only; slight success drop vs full reasoning; reasoning vs acting rather than multiple learning modalities.
Edge footprint (as published): The RL meta-policy is lightweight; the reasoning LLM's placement (local vs cloud) is not stated in the abstract.
Role in the framework: Baseline to beat / closest competing approach: RL-learned resource-aware orchestration of when to invoke expensive reasoning.

Topic: Adaptive computation, mixture of experts and routing
Task: Efficient VLA inference via dynamic layer activation for robot manipulation.
Method: Mixture-of-Layers VLA with a Spatial-Temporal Aware Router selecting layers per state, plus Cognition Self-Knowledge Distillation.
Setup and data: RLBench simulation (ten tasks) and real-world manipulation.
Key result: +8% mean success rate across ten tasks; up to 5.6x lower computational cost than standard LLMs.
Limitation: Large MLLM backbone still GPU-bound; ten tasks; distillation needed to recover capacity.
Edge footprint (as published): Billion-parameter MLLM; up to 5.6x savings still leave it beyond a Raspberry Pi 5; router logic itself is light.
Role in the framework: Competing approach / component: state-conditioned dynamic depth routing within a VLA, complementary to modality-level orchestration.

Task: Provide a large, diverse benchmark for vision-guided manipulation learning.
Method: Simulated benchmark with 100 hand-designed tasks, multi-camera observations and motion-planned demonstrations.
Setup and data: Simulated single-arm manipulator with over-the-shoulder stereo and wrist cameras.
Key result: 100 tasks with unlimited demonstrations; no performance numbers in abstract.
Limitation: Simulation only; demonstrations are motion-planned rather than human; sim-to-real gap for low-cost arms.
Edge footprint (as published): Simulator requires a desktop machine; not intended for on-robot execution.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference: common simulated testbed for comparing RL and imitation modalities.

Task: Understand what matters when learning manipulation from offline human demonstrations.
Method: Empirical study of six offline learning algorithms (BC variants and offline RL) across datasets of varying quality.
Setup and data: Five simulated and three real-world multi-stage manipulation tasks; human demonstration datasets.
Key result: Lessons on design sensitivity, demonstration quality and stopping criteria; no numbers in abstract.
Limitation: Study of existing algorithms; limited real-world tasks.
Edge footprint (as published): Policies are modest networks (tens of millions of parameters or fewer); inference plausibly CPU-feasible, training GPU-based.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference: best practices and pitfalls for imitation learning, informing behavioural-fidelity signals.

Task: Benchmark long-horizon language-conditioned manipulation.
Method: Open-source simulated benchmark with language-specified task chains and flexible sensors; multi-context imitation baseline.
Setup and data: Simulated tabletop manipulation environments; zero-shot evaluation on novel instructions and environments.
Key result: Multi-context imitation baseline performs poorly; no numbers in abstract.
Limitation: Simulation only; fixed robot embodiment.
Edge footprint (as published): Simulator needs a desktop/GPU for rendering; evaluation tool rather than on-robot component.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference: shared benchmark for efficiency-aware policies (DeeR-VLA, MoDE).

Task: Design a compact, low-cost mobile manipulator for homes.
Method: Differential-drive base, lift and telescoping arm for Cartesian end-effector motion; optional wrists and compliant gripper; stability modelling.
Setup and data: Commercial Stretch RE1 teleoperated and autonomously controlled in real homes.
Key result: Design justified analytically and by home deployments; no numbers in abstract.
Limitation: Design paper; limited quantitative evaluation of tasks.
Edge footprint (as published): Onboard computer is PC-class rather than Pi-class (not stated in abstract); platform-level reference.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference: comparable low-cost mobile manipulator platform to position LeKiwi against.

Task: Imitation learning of bimanual mobile manipulation with whole-body control.
Method: Low-cost whole-body teleoperation for data collection; behaviour cloning with co-training on static ALOHA data.
Setup and data: Mobile ALOHA real robot; household tasks (cooking, cabinet, lift, rinsing); 50 demonstrations per task.
Key result: Co-training increases success rates by up to 90% with 50 demonstrations per task.
Limitation: Task-specific policies; significant teleoperation effort; limited generalisation evidence.
Edge footprint (as published): Onboard laptop-class GPU computer rather than Pi-class; policies (ACT/diffusion-style) need more than a Pi 5 at the reported rates (not stated in abstract).
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference / baseline: low-cost mobile-manipulation imitation pipeline comparable to LeKiwi.

Task: Provide an open, end-to-end software stack for real-world robot learning.
Method: PyTorch library with policies (IL, RL, VLA), dataset format and tooling, hardware drivers and simulation integration.
Setup and data: Supports SO-100/SO-101, LeKiwi, Koch and other robots; LIBERO/MetaWorld simulation; datasets on Hugging Face Hub.
Key result: Software release; no experimental results in the repository description.
Limitation: Fast-moving codebase; contents depend on version; evaluation provided separately in Cadene 2026.
Edge footprint (as published): Library supports Pi-hosted LeKiwi hardware; heavier policies typically run on a separate GPU machine, lighter ones (e.g. ACT) are small.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: the software substrate (drivers, datasets, policy implementations) for the framework platform.

Task: Enable cross-embodiment generalist robot policies through shared data and models.
Method: Standardised multi-robot dataset; RT-X high-capacity models trained across embodiments.
Setup and data: 22 robots, 21 institutions, 527 skills, 160,266 tasks.
Key result: RT-X shows positive transfer, improving multiple robots' capabilities.
Limitation: No per-robot figures in abstract; large models; data heterogeneity.
Edge footprint (as published): RT-X models require GPU/TPU inference; not Pi-class deployable; data is reusable for pre-training.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference / competing approach: generalist cross-embodiment policy vs modality orchestration.

Task: Improve rigour of evaluation for learned robot policies.
Method: Position/methodology paper proposing reporting of conditions, complementary metrics, statistical analysis and qualitative failure descriptions.
Setup and data: Illustrative evaluation of several learned manipulation policies on physical robots.
Key result: Best-practice guidelines; no quantitative results in abstract.
Limitation: Methodological proposal; recommendations increase evaluation cost.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference: protocol and reporting standard for the framework experiments.

Task: Rigorous, sample-efficient comparison of two robot policies with few trials.
Method: Sequential statistical test with near-optimal stopping for comparing success rates, avoiding p-hacking from adaptive trial counts.
Setup and data: Numerical simulation and real-world robot manipulation experiments; multi-task simulated comparison.
Key result: Up to 32% fewer evaluation trials than state-of-the-art baselines; >160 simulation rollouts saved in a multi-task comparison.
Limitation: Pairwise binary-success comparisons; relies on trial independence.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference: statistical protocol for comparing the orchestrator against fixed-modality baselines with few real-robot trials.

Task: Rigorously evaluate multitask large behaviour models for dexterous manipulation.
Method: Diffusion-Policy-based multitask LBMs; blind, randomised statistical evaluation against single-task baselines.
Setup and data: Simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation; bimanual platforms at TRI (details not in the abstract).
Key result: Multitask pretraining improves success, robustness and data efficiency; performance scales predictably with pretraining (no figures in the abstract).
Limitation: Large-compute models; no numbers extracted.
Edge footprint (as published): Large diffusion transformers requiring GPU inference; not Pi-class deployable.
Role in the framework: Evaluation reference / baseline: rigorous evaluation protocol and evidence for pretraining in the imitation modality.

Task: Provide an integrated open-source library for end-to-end robot learning.
Method: Library spanning motor middleware, dataset collection/streaming (LeRobotDataset), training and deployment; asynchronous inference.
Setup and data: Community datasets on Hugging Face Hub; RTX 4090 profiling; real-world tasks with low-cost arms.
Key result: >16,000 datasets from >2,200 contributors; ACT ~5 ms / 211 MB vs π0 ~209 ms / 13.3 GB on RTX 4090; async 73.3% vs sync 78.3% success with 19 vs 9 cubes per 60 s.
Limitation: Profiling on desktop GPU, not embedded; limited real-world evaluation.
Edge footprint (as published): ACT-scale policies (52M params, ~211 MB) are plausible on a Pi 5 CPU at reduced rate; diffusion and π0 require a GPU per reported figures.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / evaluation reference: software stack plus latency–memory figures for candidate modality policies.

Task: Guarantee temporal-logic safety properties during RL learning and execution.
Method: Shield synthesised from a temporal-logic specification; preemptive (restricts actions) or post-posed (corrects unsafe actions) placement.
Setup and data: Several RL scenarios (details not given in abstract).
Key result: Safety enforced while preserving convergence under stated conditions; no numbers in abstract.
Limitation: Requires formal specification and finite abstraction; scalability to continuous high-dimensional dynamics.
Edge footprint (as published): Once synthesised, a shield is a lookup/automaton with negligible runtime cost; suitable for a Pi-class robot, though synthesis is offline.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse: runtime safety monitor overriding any active modality; basis for the recovery layer.

Task: Runtime assurance for neural (e.g. RL-trained) controllers.
Method: Simplex-style decision module switching between neural and verified baseline controllers, with reverse switching and online retraining of the neural controller.
Setup and data: Case studies: target-seeking ground rover in an obstacle field; artificial pancreas controller.
Key result: Safety guarantees with limited performance loss; no numbers in the abstract.
Limitation: Needs a verified baseline controller and safety region; hard for manipulation.
Edge footprint (as published): Decision module and baseline controller are lightweight; online retraining cost depends on network size; plausible on edge hardware for small controllers.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / competing approach: monitor-based switching between learned and safe controllers with learning from interventions.

Task: Review safe learning in robotics across control and RL.
Method: Literature review unifying learning-based control, safe RL and certification methods.
Setup and data: Survey of the literature.
Key result: Unified framework and open challenges; call for physics-based benchmarks.
Limitation: No new experiments; field has since advanced.
Role in the framework: Evaluation/design reference: conceptual map for safety and recovery in the orchestrator.

Task: Tutorial on data-driven safety filters for uncertain systems.
Method: Comparison of HJ reachability, control barrier functions and predictive safety filters.
Setup and data: Tutorial with an inverted-pendulum design example.
Key result: Unified treatment of three filter classes and comparative example.
Limitation: Low-dimensional example; synthesis burden for complex manipulation.
Role in the framework: Component to reuse / design reference: options for a certified safety filter beneath the orchestrator.

Task: Review and unify safety-filter methods for autonomous systems.
Method: Unified framework decomposing safety filters into monitoring and intervention across model-based and data-driven classes.
Setup and data: Literature review.
Key result: Unified modular view; directions for scalable synthesis, robust monitoring, efficient intervention.
Limitation: No empirical evaluation.
Role in the framework: Design reference: monitor–intervention decomposition as confidence signal and recovery trigger for the orchestrator.
